title: LIV Golf Three Years On: What Has It Changed and What Hasn't?
summary: The Saudi-backed breakaway tour promised to transform professional golf. Three years in, we assess what LIV has actually delivered — for the players who joined, the sport it disrupted, and the fans watching from the outside.
content:
When LIV Golf launched in 2022 with Saudi backing and prize funds that dwarfed anything the established tours offered, the professional golf world fractured. Players who had competed alongside each other for decades found themselves on opposite sides of a commercial and philosophical divide. The PGA Tour suspended its LIV members. Players who stayed loyal to the established circuit accused those who left of prioritising money over the sport's integrity. Those who joined argued they had the right to maximise their earnings in an open market.

Three years later, the fault lines remain, though the initial fury has softened into something more like uneasy coexistence. What has LIV Golf actually delivered?

The Player Experience

For the players who joined, the financial reality has been exactly as advertised. Signing fees in the tens of millions for established names. Prize funds per event that exceeded anything the PGA Tour offered for regular-season events. Guaranteed contracts that provided financial security regardless of weekly results.

The sporting reality has been more complicated. LIV's format — 54 holes, no cuts, team events alongside individual competition — is different enough from traditional strokeplay that some players have found their competitive sharpness diminished when they have competed in major championships. Others have thrived. The relationship between competitive format and peak performance remains contested.

The Majors Question

The majors — the Masters, the US Open, The Open Championship, and the PGA Championship — remained open to LIV players who met their qualification criteria. This was the critical decision that prevented LIV from becoming a complete alternative circuit and kept the sport's most prestigious events as a shared stage.

LIV players have competed in majors. Some have contended. The fear that the split would create a de facto second tier of professional golf, in which the best players competed in one circuit while the other carried reduced legitimacy, has not been fully realised — partly because the major winners have come from both sides of the divide.

I joined LIV because I believe in the product, the format, and the opportunity. But I still want to win majors. That has not changed. The major championships are where golf's history is written, and I intend to be part of that history.

What LIV Has Changed

LIV's most lasting impact may be on player compensation across the board. The PGA Tour, in response to LIV's recruitment, raised prize funds significantly and created elevated events with purses that have changed the financial calculus for players who stayed. The bidding war for talent — however uncomfortable it was for the sport's institutions — benefited players who were never going to join LIV but gained leverage from its existence.

LIV also changed conversations about golf's format. The circuit's emphasis on entertainment, on team identity, on spectator experience, has influenced how the established tours think about their own product. Some elements will be absorbed. Others will not. But golf is now a sport that has had the conversation about what a modern format should look like, and that matters.

What Hasn't Changed

The majors remain the pinnacle. The world rankings remain controversial but contested. Golf's best players still want to be identified as the best players in the world, and that identification happens through the established ranking system and the established championships. LIV, for all it has changed, has not altered golf's fundamental hierarchy of achievement.
author: SportsKeen Editorial
